#4260. Toyota is giving the Corolla a radical makeover, including its first 100% electric version

Toyota is overhauling its best-selling vehicle of all time, which will include the first fully electric Corolla.

The Toyota Corolla is one of the most recognized and best-selling automotive nameplates of all time.

Since its debut in 1966, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla thanks to its reliability, low cost of ownership, efficiency, and affordable price tag.

Toyota sells the Corolla in more than 150 countries and has expanded the lineup over the past 50 years from sedans and hatchbacks to coupes, wagons, a sporty GR Corolla, and the Corolla Cross compact SUV.

For its 13th generation, Toyota is planning a major overhaul that’s expected to be its biggest transformation yet.

The next-gen Toyota Corolla will be based on a new “multipathway” platform that will support gas, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and, for the first time, fully electric powertrains.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle ― whatever the power source ― let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive!” Toyota’s former president and current CEO Koji Sato said after unveiling the Corolla Concept at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Toyota has kept most details a secret, including battery and powertrain specs. However, the new version is expected to adopt a similar design to the concept.

“When we created the concept, we wanted to give the Corolla name a new twist,” Norihiko Kobayashi, who has led the Corolla program since 2011, told Motor.es during a recent interview.

The Corolla has undergone several minor updates over the past 60 years, but the next-gen model will look nothing like its predecessors.

“It wasn’t simply about following in the footsteps of the past,” Kobayashi explained, “we wanted to delve into the future while still maintaining the Corolla identity.”

Developing the next-gen Corolla “wasn’t just about making a new car, but about redefining the future without looking back,” he added.

Like the current version, the new Toyota Corolla will come in several different body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and a GR variant.

Zenless Zone Zero's 2.4 update is a chunky one, adding a new faction to the action RPG's roster alongside a new area, and fresh playable characters.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program was a big one, bringing us all the news about Version 2.4, the next major update. It’s called On the Precipice of the Abyss, and it will be available to download on November 26.

On the Precipice of the Abyss has tendrils in many areas of the game, touching several parts of its fiction as well as gameplay, so it’s one to watch out for.

Version 2.4’s biggest claim to fame is the introduction of the Krampus Compliance Authority, a new faction that’s affiliated with TOPS. This looks to be the oversight committee, dispatched after the squad’s adventure beneath Timesworn Hill.

The events of this narrative arch follow on from the Timesworn Hill crisis, which is partly why we’re going to a new area as part of this update. The old mining site can now be explored for the first time in a decade, now that the Miasma has begun to recede.

Our newcomers this time around are Dialyn and Banyue. Dialyn is an S-Rank Physical Stun Agent who’s a former customer service specialist. This isn’t just a backstory, however, as it plays into her gameplay.

Dialyn relies on two resources: Customer Complaint and Positive Review, but her core role is to stun enemies and allow teammates to unleash their Ults, with a nice boost to boot.

Banyue is another S-Rank, though he’s a Fire Rupture Agent. He uses his martial arts expertise to create combinations of might and grandeur. In combat, he pulls from Adrenaline and Wrathful Fires, alternating between the two to fuel his actions. There’s a bit of rhythm to his gameplay that might take you a little while to master.

Even more characters will join as part of this update, in the form of not one but two new Bangboo units. Birkblick is Krampus' own proprietary lil bunny fella, who brings a sensor array that can transform into a cannon in combat, essentially tracking and immediately nuking targets. Then there’s Bild N. Boolok, a Support Agent-affiliated Physical damage dealing Bangboo bringing a giant block hammer to the fight to, well, smash enemies with.

It’s a bit of a winter party in Version 2.4, it seems, as the update will bring back Hugo (Attack - Ice), and Ellen (Attack - Ice), too.

You can also look forward to the return of the Bangboo auto chess event, which now includes PvE stages with unique rewards. In fact, playing this event is how you could get Bild N. Boolok for free. Lightstream Notes is another event that will be available for the duration of this update, and it will let you tag along with Ye Shunguang to New Eridu.

#4258. This 1991 Mercedes-Benz 560SEC on BaT Has an Extra Bit of Euro-Snob Appeal

This big Benz is more powerful and better-looking than the U.S. version.

A Mercedes-Benz executive coupe from the early 1990s is a grand tourer par excellence, and you could hardly do better than this well-traveled machine. Currently on Bring a Trailerr (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos), this is a European-spec 1991 560SEC that was imported first to Japan before being brought to the United States seven years ago. The mileage is reasonable at the equivalent of 78K miles, but if you like to travel, here's your beast.

This generation of Mercedes coupe was the two-door sibling to the wunderbar W126 S-class, designed by the legendary Bruno Sacco. The first of these C126 coupes launched in 1981, kicking off a decade-long run that ended with the 1991 model year. These are truly great cars from the brand’s “The best or nothing” era.

See all results for used cars for sale near 63129

U.S.-market 560s came with a fairly emissions-strangled version of Mercedes's 5.5-liter V-8, but this car benefits from higher compression and slightly freer-flowing exhaust. There were more powerful versions available, but here you can expect around 275 horsepower and mountains of creamy torque, fed through a four-speed automatic gearbox.

It's not an AMG under the hood, nor are the stately looks here anywhere near as boisterous as the wide-body versions of the 560SEC that Affalterbach dreamed up. Here, the tailoring is more discreet, set off by a set of 17-inch Lorinser wheels and a slightly lower ride height on H&R springs with Bilstein dampers up front.

It looks understated and reserved in a way Mercedes doesn't really do anymore. Inside, it's just as cushy as you would hope, with leather heated seats, plenty of wood trim, and a stereo that has been updated with Bluetooth connectivity.

There’s an issue with the air conditioning that a specialist could probably address, but this example has had plenty of mechanical work done. The fuel system was overhauled with new injectors and a new distributor a few years ago, and larger work including valve seals and a new timing chain was done two years ago. At that time, perishables like vacuum lines were also replaced.

Basically, this well-fettled big coupe is an idealized version of the top-dog Mercedes from the brand’s glory days.

#4257. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:

BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, said the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete plans” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

The judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

The UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD said it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

There’s more coming. JLR also has a separate case in Rotterdam over copyright and “slavish imitation,” with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

The Ti7 looks like a Defender. We said so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

"...ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression."

Really? I feel like anyone who pays even a little attention to car designs isn't going to mistake the two. The thing most people see as differentiating within the same category is the headlights, tail lights, grill - which are all significantly different.

The only real similarity is the proportions, there are a ton of similarly proportioned SUVs but that's a result of the form factor.

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

Nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

#4255. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

#4253. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4251. Subaru is cutting EV prices by dropping one of its most distinctive features

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the company is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

It was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru said, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”

Apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing new FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

All of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

The new Subaru Uncharted (4×2) starts at €26,525 ($28,900), the Solterra (4×2) starts at €35,025 ($38,200), and the E-Outback (4×2) starts at €36,525 ($39,800) in Spain, including subsidies, discounts, and other incentives.

Preorders are open for the Uncharted, while the Solterra and E-Outback are expected to launch in mid-2027.

Will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

For a small electric car driven on pavement I prefer RWD, which offers less complexity, better uphill traction, and a tighter turning circle. I love the handling of my last two cars, a RWD Miata and a RWD BMW i3 (old style).

Subaru is already selling considerably more EVs in the US, with three affordable, practical electric SUVs: the Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker.

In Spring 2027, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getaway. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Subaru introduce a FWD option for other models, like the Solterra, at a lower price point.

Then again, AWD is used significantly more in the US than in Spain and other markets. For now, the Uncharted remains Subaru’s sole FWD model.

#4249. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4248. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."

By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

#4246. One of the world’s biggest zinc mines is getting Alaska’s largest solar farm

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

The Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review says site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

Red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the plans call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

The mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating plan. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Cost to import sun to a remote Alaskan village 0, cost to import diesel quite high.

A 500W panel weighs 60 lbs about the same as 9 gallons of diesel. 500W panel generates 750kwh of electricity a year each and every year for 20 years. 9 gallons of diesel gives you 350kwh of thermal energy which yields varying amounts of desired output.

Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

#4245. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4243. NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

Although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon

NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

#4242. The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.

These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.

Spend enough time browsing new e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.

If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.

To be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.

But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.

In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.

Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.

Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.

And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.

The problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds, or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’, despite that terminology having its own issues. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.

Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.

E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.

The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.

Motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.

But “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.

The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.

When riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.

They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.

In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.

What we have is that essentially all of these things are mopeds (i.e. Class 3 at 40km/h) and not much like bicycles at all.

It isn't surprising that allowing people to ride around unregistered mopeds, often on infrastructure shared with pedestrians, has created a lot of strife.

Quite a lot of them are actually even more extreme than that, and really more like 125cc motorbikes.

There’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.

And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.

Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.

Maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

While the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 29405

The Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

Speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the company’s earlier efforts, but the new Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

Not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

Other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 29405

Speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

While the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the new generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

Acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

The SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the new SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

With this new generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

#4240. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

#4239. Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX race for year-end merger deal before new Congress

Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX are working toward a year-end deadline to agree on their all-stock merger, according to the Financial Times. A signed deal by December 31 would land days before the new Congress, where Democrats have promised to dig into Musk’s companies, is sworn in on January 3.

The FT also named the directors negotiating for each side. Two of Tesla’s three are the same people who designed Musk’s $1 trillion pay package.

We’ve been tracking the Tesla-SpaceX merger since Musk first floated it in May, when we called it Musk’s fourth billion-dollar self-deal, and his first trillion-dollar self-deal. Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX could announce the deal as soon as December. The FT report adds a deadline, names and a vote threshold.

According to the FT, the talks are “moving towards a potential year-end deadline,” even though people familiar with the negotiations say an agreement isn’t close. The combined group would be worth about $3.5 trillion, by far the largest merger ever.

The new Congress is seated on January 3. As of November 24, AP’s count has Democrats at 258 House seats and 56 Senate seats. Democrats haven’t been subtle about what comes next: Sen. Ruben Gallego tagged Musk on X with “See you in January,” and SpaceX’s military contracts and Musk’s Starlink decisions over Ukraine are expected to be early investigation targets.

It’s not only Washington. Texas’ incoming attorney general told Bloomberg that a merger of this size “warrants tremendous scrutiny,” and Bloomberg had previously reported that the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

Tesla’s special committee is chair Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung, advised by Evercore. SpaceX is represented by Roelof Botha and Randy Glein, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as advisers. Both banks also helped take SpaceX public in June.

Denholm and Wilson-Thompson should sound familiar. They were the two-person special committee that built Musk’s new CEO pay package after a Delaware judge voided his 2018 award. And that 2025 award has change-in-control terms that drop its operational milestones and vest earned shares at the deal price, so the committee that wrote it is now negotiating the deal that could trigger it.

Ira Ehrenpreis, a long-time friend of Musk, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees and has sat on SpaceX’s board since February, isn’t on Tesla’s committee, per the FT.

If you can believe it, Musk isn’t formally in the room. The FT says Texas governance rules keep him out of active negotiations, but both committees can consult senior executives for information. Every one of those executives reports to Musk.

Any agreement goes to a separate extraordinary Tesla shareholder meeting, and it needs more than 50% of all outstanding votes, not just of votes cast. Abstentions and uncast shares effectively count as “no.”

That sounds like a high bar. But Musk holds about 20% of Tesla’s voting power, and nothing in the report says his shares will be excluded. If they count, he’s 40% of the way to approval before a single other shareholder votes. On the other side, Musk controls about 84% of SpaceX’s votes, so there’s no real suspense there.

Uncast retail votes are exactly what Tesla’s new auto-vote program, rolled out in its October proxy, was designed to reduce.

Then there’s the regulatory side. The FT says the deal could draw scrutiny in the US, China, Europe and the UK, with Tesla’s China operations sitting awkwardly next to SpaceX’s rocket and Starlink business, which does a lot of work for the US military. Giga Shanghai builds more than half of Tesla’s cars.

Congress can’t block this merger. Antitrust review sits with Trump’s DOJ and FTC until 2029, plus China, the EU and the UK.

It's probably already too late to escape Jan 3. The DoJ investigation into the merger will take a minimum of a few months. At the very least it looks like there is a 30 mandatory waiting period, so if the merger isn't announced by Dec 4, that 30 days takes them to Jan 3. That gives them 10 calendar days to finish negotiations and get stock holder approval and they have to give time for the voters to get their votes in. So short of some miracle, Musk isn't going to get this done before Jan 3 ... at least from my understanding and counting.

What congressional committees can do is subpoena. Committee minutes, the Evercore fairness work, emails between Denholm’s committee and Musk’s executives about how the exchange ratio got set. That’s the kind of record that got Musk’s 2018 pay package voided by a Delaware judge, and it’s the kind of record nobody wants dragged into a hearing mid-negotiation.

The talks are “not close,” yet there’s a deadline. When the deadline comes from the political calendar instead of the negotiation, the side that wants to close fast is the one giving ground. But in this case, Musk is both sides, but he is mainly SpaceX.

We’ve said it before, and we’ll keep saying it: the only vote that means anything here is a majority of Tesla shareholders not named Musk. Denholm, who is up for re-election at next week’s December 3 annual meeting, could commit to that today, but in her entire tenure as Tesla chair, she always did exactly what Musk wanted.

Whatever happens to Tesla’s corporate structure, the cheapest way to fuel an EV is still sunlight on your own roof. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4237. Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.

Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role

"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."

The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal

The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."

#4236. Nuro pulls safety drivers from Lucid Gravity Uber robotaxis in Bay Area

Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat. The driverless testing starts in four Peninsula and South Bay cities, with a fleet of more than 100 Gravity SUVs delivered by Lucid for the program.

It’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership. But it comes with a quieter update: the public launch, originally promised for 2026, is now expected in Q1 2027.

According to Nuro’s announcement, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year. Uber employees will “soon” be able to ride in the driverless vehicles.

Nuro has run the Gravity robotaxis around the clock in the Bay Area and Houston since December 2025, but always with a safety driver. Before pulling the driver, the company says it ran no-vehicle-operator testing at its Las Vegas closed course, covering things like pedestrian encounters and right-of-way violations, plus large-scale simulation.

Tilo Schwarz, Nuro’s head of the Nuro Driver, pointed out that driverless operation “isn’t new” for the company. That’s fair. Nuro has run driverless delivery pods in California since 2020. But this is its first time doing it with a passenger vehicle.

The regulatory pieces were already in place. As we reported in May, the California DMV extended Nuro’s driverless testing permit to the Lucid Gravity, and the CPUC followed with a drivered pilot permit for carrying passengers.

Nuro says it’s one of just six companies allowed to test without a driver on California roads. The DMV’s list, last updated November 5, confirms it: AutoMo, Nuro, Tensor, Waymo, WeRide, and Zoox.

Tesla isn’t one of them. Its “Tesla Robotaxi LLC” entity only holds a permit to test with a driver in California, and it has no deployment permit either.

Waymo, of course, is the benchmark. It already runs a paid, fully driverless service across much of the Bay Area, including the Peninsula and South Bay where Nuro is just now pulling its safety drivers.

When Lucid, Nuro, and Uber announced the program in July 2025, the plan was to launch “later next year” in a major US city. As recently as June, when Uber named Houston as the second market for mid-2027, the Bay Area launch was still slated for this year.

Now it’s Q1 2027. Not a huge slip, but it’s a slip.

The scale ambition has gone the other way. Uber’s purchase commitment grew from 20,000 vehicles to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles with the Nuro Driver, starting with the Gravity and later Lucid’s upcoming midsize models. Uber will own and operate the cars with fleet partners, and they’ll only be available through the Uber app.

For context, Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3 2026. At that pace, 35,000 robotaxis would take more than two years of Lucid’s entire output.

This is real progress, and it deserves credit. Nuro got the permits, built a formal safety case, tested at a closed course, and only then took the driver out. That’s how it should be done, and it should be applauded, especially as some companies claim to lead in autonomy while being too chicken to get a permit in California.

But let’s keep it in perspective. Driverless testing in four suburban cities with a 100-car fleet is where Waymo was years ago. Waymo is already doing hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week, including in the same part of the Bay Area. Nuro and Uber aren’t catching up to Waymo in 2027.

The bigger question for me is Lucid. The partnership gives Lucid exactly the kind of volume it needs, and 35,000 vehicles is a big number for a company delivering under 4,000 cars a quarter.

If this program is successful, and that’s a big if, then it could really help Lucid get to its more affordable vehicle.

#4235. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.
